title: How to choose your first AI use case
description: A practical way to find an AI opportunity with a clear business owner, usable information and a result your team can evaluate.
answer: Choose a specific workflow with a recognised business problem, an accountable owner, and information you can use. Compare candidate use cases on value, feasibility, review effort, consequences of error, and adoption. Establish the current baseline and define the decision a pilot must support before choosing tools or committing to a build.
author: Authentia
body:
Your first AI initiative sets expectations for everything that follows. A useful starting point should address a problem people recognise, fit the information you can actually access, and give your team a clear way to judge the result. An impressive demonstration can help secure attention. A well-chosen piece of work can help secure a better business decision.

We recommend starting with a specific workflow and its owner. The question is where AI could improve the work enough to justify the effort of changing it.

Describe the work before choosing the technology

Replace broad ambitions such as “use AI in operations” with a description of what happens today. What starts the process? Who receives the request? Which information do they consult? What do they produce, and who checks it? Include the handoffs and exceptions that make the work difficult.

“Help account managers prepare for customer reviews” is still broad. “Prepare a review brief from approved account notes and service records for the account manager to check” gives a team something concrete to explore. It identifies the inputs, output and person responsible for using it.

Look for a worthwhile, manageable starting point

Build a shortlist with the people who do the work. Ask them where time disappears, where requests wait and where information has to be assembled repeatedly. Then examine each candidate against the same questions:

  • Business value: What would improve for the customer, employee or organisation if this worked?
  • Information: Are the required sources available, current and suitable for the intended use?
  • Judgement: Can a qualified person recognise a good result and identify a bad one?
  • Consequences: What could happen if the output were incomplete or wrong?
  • Ownership: Who can make decisions, provide examples and change the workflow?
  • Adoption: Will the result arrive where people already work, in a form they can use?

These are discussion prompts, rather than a universal scoring formula. A high-value idea with inaccessible information may belong on a later roadmap. A modest opportunity with a committed owner can make a more informative first trial.

Establish what improvement would mean

Observe the current process before setting a target. Include preparation, waiting, checking, correction and follow-up. A faster first draft has limited value if it creates more work for the reviewer.

Choose measures that reflect the actual job. Depending on the workflow, these might include total handling time, completeness, missed information, escalation quality or whether employees can find the answer they need. Record what you know and which assumptions still need testing. Treat estimated benefits as estimates until the workflow has been evaluated.

An illustrative choice

Consider a fictional equipment distributor comparing two ideas: an assistant that answers customers directly, and an internal assistant that prepares product information for a sales specialist. Both might use similar reference material, but they create different responsibilities.

The internal option lets the specialist check sources and correct the draft before anything reaches a customer. It also exposes gaps in the product information. The direct-response option requires additional decisions about permitted answers, unusual requests, escalation and service ownership.

The internal assistant could therefore be the better first investigation, provided preparation is a meaningful burden. That conclusion would come from the workflow and its constraints. It would not establish that internal tools are always preferable or that this particular idea will deliver a return.

Give the first initiative a clear boundary

A short decision brief should state the problem, intended users, permitted inputs, expected output and review process. Include what the trial will leave out. For example, drafting an account brief need not include updating customer records or sending messages.

Name the business owner and the person responsible for evaluation. Identify the decision the trial must support: proceed, adjust the scope, investigate another option or stop. This gives the implementation team a useful brief and gives leadership a basis for reviewing the evidence.

For a broader approach to considering trustworthiness throughout an AI system’s lifecycle, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework is a useful voluntary reference. The selection approach above is our practical recommendation, rather than a certification checklist.

title: What an AI pilot needs to prove before rollout
description: Evaluate the whole workflow, including exceptions, review effort and ownership, before expanding an AI pilot.
answer: Before wider rollout, an AI pilot should demonstrate useful performance against the current workflow on representative inputs, including missing information and exceptions. Evaluate the finished output after human review, total operating effort and cost, and whether intended users can operate it. Name owners and agree conditions for expansion, revision, or stopping.
author: Authentia
body:
A pilot should help leadership make a decision. It should show whether an AI-supported workflow is useful under the conditions the business expects to encounter, and what would need to change before wider use.

A polished demonstration answers a narrower question: can this approach produce a convincing result on the examples shown? That is a useful beginning. A rollout decision needs evidence about quality, effort, exceptions and the people who will own the service.

Agree on the decision before running the trial

Write down what the pilot is intended to establish. Be specific about its users, information sources, permitted actions and operating conditions. An internal drafting assistant and a system that sends customer responses need different evaluation plans, even if both produce similar text.

Set decision criteria with the business owner and the people responsible for delivery. Describe acceptable performance, issues that would block expansion and uncertainties that need further investigation. Agree how evidence will be reviewed before the team becomes invested in a particular result.

Compare against the current workflow

Evaluate the work people need to complete. If the system drafts a response, consider the finished response after checking and correction. If it retrieves information, examine whether the person can verify and use that information.

Compare the proposed process with the current one using similar work. Include the time spent preparing inputs, resolving errors and dealing with cases the system cannot handle. Capture the quality of the existing process as well. The comparison should reflect the actual alternative available to the business.

Use examples that reveal the limits

Build a test set from representative work, using information approved for that purpose. Include routine examples and cases that experienced employees find difficult. Keep some examples separate from those used to refine the prompts or configuration, so the final check includes work the team has not repeatedly tuned against.

A practical evaluation should investigate:

  • Ordinary work: Does the system produce a useful result on the requests expected most often?
  • Missing information: Does it identify what is unavailable, or present an unsupported answer?
  • Conflicting sources: Does it expose the disagreement and direct the user to an appropriate next step?
  • Unusual requests: Does the workflow recognise when the task falls outside its intended scope?
  • Service interruption: Can people continue working when an integration or information source is unavailable?
  • Repeated runs: Are results sufficiently consistent for this particular job?

Review both the output and what happened in connected systems. A message saying an action succeeded is insufficient evidence that the intended record was updated correctly.

An illustrative pilot review

Imagine a fictional services company testing an assistant that prepares project handover notes. The routine examples look clear and well structured. Reviewers then test records containing an unresolved client request and conflicting delivery dates.

The important question becomes whether the assistant preserves those uncertainties and makes them visible. A fluent handover that quietly chooses a date could create more operational difficulty than an incomplete draft that asks for clarification.

The team might decide to continue with mandatory review and a narrower set of source documents. It might instead pause to improve the underlying records. Either decision could be a useful pilot outcome. The trial has exposed a dependency that a presentation alone would not resolve.

Test whether people can operate it

Ask intended users to complete the workflow with the guidance they would receive after rollout. Observe where they hesitate, what they trust and which checks they skip. A process that depends on the pilot’s designer standing beside every user needs more work before expansion.

Confirm who maintains the reference information, handles exceptions and reviews proposed changes. Include recurring service costs, support and review effort in the operating picture. Passing a quality check does not establish that the business is ready to run the service.

Make the conclusion specific

A useful pilot readout explains what was tested, what passed, what failed and what remains unknown. Recommend a defined next step, with an owner and conditions for proceeding. Expand the proven scope gradually and revisit the evidence when the workflow, model or source information changes.

For a technical treatment of task design, grading and observed outcomes, see Anthropic’s guide to evaluating AI agents. Its developer-focused methods provide useful context; the evaluation plan still needs to reflect your business workflow.

Authentia provides implementation advisory to help client teams and delivery partners define these checks and turn pilot evidence into a clear rollout decision.

title: Should you buy, adapt or build your AI solution?
description: Compare ready-made software, configured tools and custom development against the workflow, operating effort and ownership your business needs.
answer: Buy when an existing product fits the workflow and operating requirements. Adapt when available tools need configuration, approved information, or a different handoff. Build when distinct requirements justify the additional ownership. Compare all three routes against the same brief, representative tasks, total costs, access controls, maintenance responsibilities, and ability to change direction.
author: Authentia
body:
Choosing an AI solution is also a decision about how your organisation will operate it. A subscription, a configured workflow and a custom application create different responsibilities for your team. The right choice depends on the work, the information involved and the value of doing something differently.

We recommend comparing three routes against the same business brief: buy an existing product, adapt available tools, or build a custom application. Keep the desired outcome consistent while you examine what each route would require.

Buy when an existing product fits the work

Start by examining capabilities in software your team already uses, alongside relevant specialist products. An existing product may offer a suitable workflow, familiar administration and a supported path for routine updates.

Test the actual fit. Can it use the information your employees need? Does it respect the access boundaries you require? Can reviewers inspect the result and correct it? What happens when a request does not fit the product’s normal process?

A feature list is useful for shortlisting. A representative task is more useful for deciding whether the product supports your way of working. Record the changes your business would need to make to use it successfully.

Adapt when the pieces exist but the workflow differs

Adaptation might involve configuring an assistant, connecting approved information sources, changing prompts or linking existing tools. It can be appropriate when a standard product comes close but needs a particular handoff, output format or review stage.

Make the remaining responsibilities visible. Someone still needs to maintain the configuration, manage access, update source material and check that changes have not affected the result. A workflow assembled from available tools needs an owner just as a custom application does.

Ask the delivery team to explain which parts are standard, which are configured and which contain custom logic. That distinction helps you understand where support will come from and what knowledge your own team needs.

Build when the distinct requirements justify ownership

A custom application can make sense when the required workflow, integration or user experience cannot be met adequately through existing options. It may also be justified when the capability is central to how the business serves its customers.

Building an application does not necessarily mean training a model. A delivery team may build around existing model services and concentrate on information access, workflow, evaluation and the interface people use. Google Cloud’s application development guidance describes prompt design and additional customisation as separate considerations, and notes that further model customisation may be unnecessary when prompts already produce suitable responses.

The business still needs a plan for ongoing ownership. Ask who will support integrations, test updates, investigate failures and maintain documentation after the initial delivery team leaves.

Compare the complete working arrangement

Use a common set of questions for every option. This keeps a polished product presentation and a custom development proposal comparable.

  • Workflow fit: Which parts of the job are supported, and what remains manual?
  • Information: Which sources are accessible, and how are they kept current?
  • Quality: How will the option be tested on your work, including exceptions?
  • Control: Who can change the behaviour, inspect activity and stop an action?
  • Operating effort: Who will maintain, review and support it?
  • Cost: What are the setup, usage, integration, support and internal time commitments?
  • Change: How difficult would it be to move information or the workflow elsewhere?

Distinguish confirmed capabilities from planned features and assumptions. Where an important answer is uncertain, request a targeted test rather than treating the uncertainty as resolved.

An illustrative comparison

Consider a fictional distributor that wants sales staff to prepare answers to product questions. A feature in its existing software might be sufficient for summarising account notes. Answering detailed compatibility questions could require a maintained product reference source and a specialist review step.

The team should first establish whether an available product can support that source and review process. If it can, configuration may be enough. If it cannot, a custom interface or integration may be worth investigating. The decision turns on the missing capability and its value, rather than a general preference for buying or building.

Record why the chosen route is appropriate

Write a short decision record: the outcome sought, alternatives considered, evidence gathered and responsibilities accepted. Include the assumptions that would change the decision. This makes the choice easier to revisit when business needs or available products change.

Authentia’s AI strategy work helps leadership compare routes before committing. Our implementation guidance helps the selected client team or delivery partner work from a clear, testable brief.

title: From a useful prompt to a reliable business workflow
description: Give reusable prompts the inputs, reference material, review steps and ownership they need to support everyday work.
answer: Turn a useful prompt into a repeatable workflow by defining its job, required inputs, approved reference material, output format, and boundaries. Give users a review checklist and a next step for missing or conflicting information. Assign an owner, keep versions, and test representative examples whenever the prompt, tool, or source information changes.
author: Authentia
body:
A useful prompt often begins as an individual discovery. Someone finds a way to produce a helpful draft, shares the wording and encourages colleagues to try it. The next challenge is making the approach useful across different people, inputs and situations.

The prompt is one part of that work. A repeatable business workflow also needs clear inputs, suitable reference information, checks and a person responsible for the result. You can define those parts before considering a more elaborate implementation.

Specify the job and the point of use

Describe what the prompt should help a person accomplish. “Summarise this document” leaves a great deal open. “Prepare a handover brief for the colleague taking over this account” creates a clearer purpose, audience and standard for relevance.

State where the output will go. A private working note can tolerate different phrasing from a customer message. A draft intended to support a decision needs to make missing information and uncertainty visible to the person making that decision.

Keep the task narrow enough that users can recognise when they have the right inputs and when the result is ready for review.

Make the reusable parts explicit

A practical prompt template should separate the instructions that stay the same from the information that changes for each task. Give users a short guide explaining what to provide and what to leave out.

  • Purpose: The job the output should support and who will use it.
  • Inputs: The records, notes or questions needed for this run.
  • Reference material: The approved information the answer should draw on.
  • Boundaries: What the assistant should avoid deciding or inventing.
  • Output: The sections or fields the reviewer needs.
  • Uncertainty: How to identify missing, ambiguous or conflicting information.

Keep the instructions direct. Add examples when they clarify a difficult expectation. Explain why an example is useful, so employees understand the judgement behind the format rather than copying its wording mechanically.

Maintain the information around the prompt

Instructions cannot resolve every problem in the source material. An outdated product sheet, an incomplete account record or competing versions of a procedure can make the task unclear.

Identify which sources are authoritative and who maintains them. Give users a way to see which material informed the result where the implementation supports it. Ask reviewers to check the underlying information when the output makes a material claim.

Also distinguish between providing information for a task and teaching a system a permanent fact. Users should know which material needs to accompany each run and which approved sources the tool can already access.

Define a review people can actually perform

“Check the answer” is a weak instruction unless the reviewer knows what to inspect. Build a short checklist around the job: are the relevant facts present, are unsupported claims absent, are uncertainties visible, and does the output meet the intended purpose?

Set a clear next step when a check fails. The reviewer might supply a missing record, correct the draft directly or refer the issue to a specialist. Repeatedly asking the system to try again is not a substitute for resolving an information gap.

For workflows that can take action, identify the point at which a person authorises that action. Treat preparing a proposed update and applying the update as separate responsibilities.

An illustrative handover workflow

Imagine a fictional operations team preparing cover notes before an employee goes on leave. The template requests current responsibilities, upcoming deadlines and unresolved decisions. It asks for a brief arranged around those categories and flags gaps for the departing employee to check.

The employee supplies approved notes, reviews the draft against the checklist and confirms the handover with the receiving colleague. Feedback may reveal that a field is unclear or an important exception is missing. The team can then improve the template and guidance together. This is a proposed workflow, rather than a claim about a delivered client result.

Keep versions and test changes

Assign an owner to the shared template. Keep a small set of representative examples and expected review criteria. When the prompt, tool or reference material changes, run those examples again and inspect the results before distributing the update.

For a technical perspective, Anthropic’s Building effective agents distinguishes predefined workflows from systems that direct their own actions. That distinction is useful when deciding how much flexibility a business task needs. A straightforward, reviewed sequence may be sufficient.

Our practical resources and prompt packs provide starting points to adapt to your work. For ongoing help reviewing priorities, usage and changes, Authentia’s ongoing advisory supports the people responsible for making those workflows useful.
